extracted.intended_audience: aspiring stand-up comedians, comedy writers, and performers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and terminology for writing jokes, structuring routines, and performing stand-up (timing, delivery, joke mechanics, material grading, and stagecraft). Useful for comedians preparing open-mic to club shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughs Per Minute (LPM)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughs Per Minute. 5 or more laughs per minute is the professional standard for stand-up comedy shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure your routine's effectiveness by laughs per minute; a great routine should get at least 5 LPMs.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABCs material rating system
rubrics_metrics.description: A rating system that gives values to jokes within routines, or routines within shows with A being the best, B second-best, and C weakest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ABCs to classify material: start with B material, use C in the middle, and close with A material. Example workflow: rehearse and record shows, then rate each joke using ABCs to optimize placement and selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: BCAs ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: The most effective order for placing jokes within routines or routines within shows: B material first, C material in the middle, and A material to close.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a show feels weaker at the end, reorder using BCAs so you end with your best jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine length preparedness (3-5 and 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common routine lengths (in minutes) comedians should have prepared and ready to perform on request: 3–5 and 10 minutes are the three most common lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always have material that fits common time slots (3–5 and 10 minutes) so you can accept a variety of bookings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing / Comic timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The tempo and rhythm developed between the comedian and the audience while performing; tempo, rhythm, and emphasis of material and response in a feedback loop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing affects setup-to-punchline delivery; great performers develop timing from live feedback. See also 'delivery'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Style of intonation, inflection, pace, timing, and character idiosyncrasies in presenting comedy material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delivery is as important as written material—intonation, pace, and character choices can make or break jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke structure — 5 mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Greg Dean model: five mechanisms that connect the Setup and Punchline — 1st Story, Target Assumption, Connector, Reinterpretation, and 2nd Story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These five mechanisms explain how jokes create surprise; study and apply them to construct reliable setups and punchlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connector
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke-structure mechanism defined as one thing with at least two interpretations; the central mechanism at the heart of jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design setups with a Connector (ambiguity) that supports multiple interpretations; the punchline exploits an unexpected interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target Assumption (TA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The expected interpretation of the Connector established by the Setup to create misdirection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setups should establish a believable Target Assumption to guide the audience away from the punchline's reinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The unexpected interpretation of the Connector that is expressed in the Punchline to create surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write punchlines that offer a compatible but unexpected alternative interpretation to the setup's TA; this surprise generates the laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1st Story
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene imagined in the audience's minds based on receiving a joke's Setup (one of the five mechanisms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft setups that create a clear, believable 1st Story so the TA and subsequent surprise will land.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2nd Story
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene imagined in the audience's minds based on receiving a joke's Punchline (one of the five mechanisms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punchlines should evoke a coherent 2nd Story that makes the reinterpretation sensible and funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected vs Unexpected interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Expected interpretation becomes the Target Assumption; unexpected (alternative) interpretation becomes the Reinterpretation and creates surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly engineer expectation in setups and then deliver a plausible but surprising alternative to maximize laugh value.

rubrics_metrics.name: TCR (Target Assumption, Connector, Reinterpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviation for Target Assumption, Connector, and Reinterpretation — a compact way to reference the core components of Greg Dean's joke structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use TCR as a shorthand during writing and editing to ensure a setup, ambiguity, and punchline reinterpretation are present and coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity as a joke-writing tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything open to more than one interpretation; in joke structure, an ambiguity (usually in setups) becomes the Connector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create productive ambiguity in setups to allow at least two plausible interpretations; that ambiguity is the raw material for the punchline's surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misdirection
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of steering the audience's thinking away from the actual punchline (often via establishing a Target Assumption).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good setups misdirect effectively; avoid telegraphing, which gives away the punchline instead of misdirecting from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telegraphing (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Causing the audience to guess the Punchline before it's delivered, usually due to too much information in the Setup or an acting choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid telegraphing by trimming setup information and altering acting choices so the punchline remains unexpected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hack / Hacky / Comic's clichés (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Overused topics, premises, and jokes filled with common comic clichés that betray a lack of original thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hacky material and clichés; originality and fresh angles are valued. 'Hack' denotes poor material or delivery and should be eliminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clapter vs Laughs (audience agreement vs humor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clapter: joke designed to get audience applause/approval rather than laughter; often used negatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware when material drives agreement (clapter) instead of true comedic surprise; prioritize laughs over applause for stronger comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edgy material and the hurt line
rubrics_metrics.description: Edgy comedy deals with hurtful subjects while maintaining a comedic tone; the 'hurt line' is the boundary where edgy crosses into drama or cruelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edgy topics can be funny if handled skillfully; ensure tone keeps the material comedic and avoids crossing the hurt line into dramatized harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material suitability: clean, blue, x-rated
rubrics_metrics.description: Classifications of material by appropriateness: clean material (suitable for network TV), blue material (risqué/sexual/swearing), x-rated (graphic/explicit, unsuitable for network TV).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor material to venue and audience; network TV requires clean material, while clubs may allow blue or x-rated material depending on the room and crowd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hammock (placement strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique of placing weak or new material between two strong jokes or routines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hammocks to try out new lines or protect weaker bits by sandwiching them between proven jokes (see BCAs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closer / Closing line (end strong)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final joke or routine designed to get the biggest laugh and end the show on a high note.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve your best (A) material for the closer to leave a strong final impression; closers are strategic and often crafted carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warm up (pre-show and show-start crowd unification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a show: physical or ritual warm-ups; at the beginning of shows: working the crowd with material or crowd work to unify the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use warm-ups and opening crowd work to build a feedback loop and prepare the audience for the next acts; it helps set tone and energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowd work
rubrics_metrics.description: Asking questions of the audience and bantering to find laughs; working the room live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowd work can engage and energize audiences; be prepared with sensitivity and quick wit for unpredictable interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Callback
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeating a punchline or reference from an earlier joke later in the routine to generate an additional laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Callbacks reward attentive audiences and can create escalating laughs when timed well; use them to build set cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catchphrase as trademark
rubrics_metrics.description: A phrase repeatedly delivered with unusual emphasis that becomes a comedian's verbal trademark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong catchphrase can become an identifying trademark, but avoid overuse that can feel gimmicky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a gag file and empirical graphing
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping an organized collection of jokes (gag file) and using visual graphs to evaluate joke effectiveness and placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record shows, collect material in a gag file, and plot performance data (graph) to empirically determine which jokes belong where in a set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Throw away (performance emphasis choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing little performing emphasis on jokes that are usually considered important (a deliberate low-emphasis delivery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use throw-away delivery strategically to change audience expectations or land a different kind of laugh; it's a performance choice rather than a content failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stagecraft rules: respect 'get the light' and avails
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Get the light' is the stage signal that time is almost up; 'avails' (availability dates) inform bookers when you can accept gigs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect stage signals (exit when you get the light) and maintain accurate availability for professionalism and booking reliability.
